title: Russia-Ukraine war: Nine Zimbabweans caught trying to leave South Africa to join conflict
description: Nine Zimbabweans have been arrested in South Africa after they were caught allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia an
body: Nine Zimbabweans have been arrested in South Africa after they were caught allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia and the Ukraine, police say.The group, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in and around Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team on Sunday evening.They were caught as they were "preparing to board flights out of the country", authorities added, but their final destination is unclear.They have been charged with contravening South Africa's Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which outlaws mercenary activity without government permission.Police said five people were arrested at South Africa's biggest airport, OR Tambo, and another four at a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team that involved Interpol.All nine later appeared in court, according to state prosecutors.The police statement added that the involvement of Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies indicated that the suspects had also allegedly violated laws in their respective home countries, prompting cooperation with South African authorities.They have also not said whether the group allegedly intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine nor provided details of the organisations allegedly involved in facilitating their travel.Citizens of several African countries, including Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, have gone to fight for Russia in Ukraine - some they had been duped and had not realised where they were going.A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.Kenya at the time estimated that 252 citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia. In March, Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue.He said at the time that an agreement had been reached to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.In March, Zimbabwe said that 15 of its nationals had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia in Ukraine, with more than 60 still trapped on the frontlines.The previous month, South Africa secured the return of 17 South Africans who were allegedly tricked into joining the war. In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.

schema.headline: Russia-Ukraine war: Nine Zimbabweans caught trying to leave South Africa to join conflict

title: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
description: France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges a
body: France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers across the country last month.Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions.Iran has yet to respond officially, but some Iranian media outlets have dismissed the allegations as baseless.The French hacking, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food in France was followed by a similar attack against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act". France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.The Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year. If the IRGC carried out the cyber-attacks, it remains unclear whether they were part of Iran's deterrence strategy.On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe. Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.Additional reporting by Farshad Bayan, BBC Persian.

schema.headline: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking

title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case
description: Prosecutors in the closely watched case alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and
body: Prosecutors in the closely watched case alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home.After weeks of emotional testimony, the jury took a week to deliberate, repeatedly telling the judge that they could not reach a verdict. The deadlock stemmed from a lone juror who voted to convict Clancy of first-degree murder, while the 11 other jurors intended to acquit Clancy by reason of insanity.In Massachusetts, as well as in all US criminal murder trials, juries must reach a unanimous decision to convict or acquit a defendant. Because the jurors failed to unanimously agree on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law, the judge declared a mistrial on 4 September, which means that she was neither found guilty nor not guilty.Clancy is currently being housed in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts. Ana Faguy contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case

title: Canary Islands: 39 dead after migrant boat sinks off Senegal en route to Europe
description: Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told the AFP news agency that all the bodies recovered by Sunday evening were Senegale
body: Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told the AFP news agency that all the bodies recovered by Sunday evening were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.Four bodies were recovered on Monday morning in an advanced state of decomposition and buried following a collective funeral prayer organised by the fire service.Rescue teams are searching along a 25km (15-mile)- stretch of coastline, but operations have been complicated by difficult access and strong ocean currents, which are pushing bodies further south.Authorities say 24 of the 39 victims have been identified and their bodies returned to their families, while 11 others are still awaiting identification.President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not to risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys."We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.This amounts to almost a third of the population on the island, one of the main entry points into Europe for migrants arriving from West Africa. Fernando Clavijo, president of the Canary Islands regional government, described the situation as "absolutely unsustainable," reports the Reuters news agency.The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency. The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.

schema.headline: Canary Islands: 39 dead after migrant boat sinks off Senegal en route to Europe

title: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
description: Figure caption, Fire engulfed Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat in Bavaria last monthByBethany Bellin BavariaPerched on a ridge high up in the
body: Figure caption, Fire engulfed Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat in Bavaria last monthByBethany Bellin BavariaPerched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.Image source, Galerie Bilderwelt/Getty ImagesImage caption, Adolf Hitler used the mountain retreat to welcome guestsBefore it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.Image source, Universal Images Group via Getty ImagesImage caption, Before it was burned down, the Kehlsteinhaus or Eagle's Nest had long been a tourist destination in BavariaAround 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history."It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler killed himself: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police say the old Nazi retreat was largely destroyed by last month's fireBut Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus."We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed."We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".Image source, ERIC SCHWAB/AFPImage caption, After Hitler's downfall, US soldiers captured the mountain-top retreat and are seen relaxing here on 4 May 1945Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question"."I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era. With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

schema.headline: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat

title: Inside the French drug gangs recruiting children to kill
description: Figure caption, Watch: "It destroys people, but we all make our own choices" - Marseille drug-gang members talk to BBCByJames WaterhouseParis correspo
body: Figure caption, Watch: "It destroys people, but we all make our own choices" - Marseille drug-gang members talk to BBCByJames WaterhouseParis correspondentWarning: Strong language and descriptions of sexual violenceAlthough she had just bought hashish from a drug dealer, the woman decided to call the police.It was because, along with the illegal drugs, she had been handed a note by the young seller during their brief meeting on a Marseille housing estate in 2022."We're being held captive and need help. We are 15-years-old," it read.The teenage dealer, a French court heard earlier this year, was one of two boys being held by a gang which they had both initially approached looking for paid work - albeit illegal.One boy had been tasked with handling money, the other worked streets around the Frais-Vallon estate. Soon though, bosses had accused them of being responsible for "shortfalls" in takings.What followed were regular beatings, the court was told, and being forced to dance naked in front of a camera as a form of blackmail. One of the boys was also raped.Hours after the woman was passed the note, the two teenagers had tried to escape from a second-storey window, injuring themselves in the process. One managed to get away, while the other was caught, beaten and stabbed, but survived.Arrests were made. Photos on the phone of one of the boys' alleged torturers showed several other young men in a similarly distressed condition. Six men have since been handed hefty sentences for what happened to the two teenagers.The boys' story highlights the grip that drug gangs hold over parts of France's second city.While the blend of Mediterranean culture, street art and hip-hop scene has made Marseille a popular tourist destination - beyond the city centre, it is another story.After months of trying, a BBC team managed to enter this dangerous world - centred on deprived streets and high-rise housing estates in the port city, which police do not enter lightly.We found an environment where ruthless gangs lure vulnerable young people with promises of easy money, but end up trapping them in a world of drug dealing, brutality and exploitation.We saw how gangs use social media to recruit hitmen and spoke to several young men caught up in the violence. From prison, one gang member accused of involvement in several murders explained how his "cold-bloodedness" had helped him rise through the ranks.Image source, Social mediaImage caption, A still image from one of DZ Mafia's notorious video statementsThe city's most powerful gang, DZ Mafia, emerged victorious from a bloody turf war and is now one of the most feared criminal organisations in France.DZ is the official internet country code for Algeria, where one of the gang's founders, a French-Algerian called Mehdi Laribi, was detained earlier this year under a French arrest warrant.The criminal outfit rose to prominence in 2023, when it became the first French gang to capitalise on its notoriety by releasing video statements - using social media to market itself as a brand - says the head of the country's anti-drug trafficking unit, Dimitri Zoulas.Its most recent statement came in July, when the mayor of a nearby town had to be placed in police protection, after intelligence suggested he was in danger of being targeted by the group.In an online video, six masked men dressed in black stood behind a table - as one of them read a statement denying DZ Mafia's involvement.Inside Marseille's drug gangs - watch on YouTube now, externalFrance's expanding illegal drugs market - which has seen a surge in cocaine imports alongside high volumes of cannabis and synthetic drugs - has also helped the gang grow rapidly.The number of cocaine users in France is expected soon to reach two million, says Zoulas, up from 600,000 in 2017. Drug smuggling across France generates €7bn (£5.9bn) a year, involving 200,000 people, he adds.Many of those distributing the drugs are children and the authorities say the number of minors caught up in trafficking is increasing. During 2025, more than 10,000 children were involved in some way, according to official figures.DZ Mafia is a prime example. To reach more customers, it needs more gang members - more children.We have found it is now recruiting young people from across France - not just to sell drugs, but to carry out kidnap, torture and murder.They are a generation seen as easy to corrupt, but also expendable, by the kingpins who typically control them from prison or overseas.And, as police and judges warn, once these children enter Marseille's underworld, it is very hard to get them out.Image source, Lea Guedj / BBCImage caption, Karine was called by a doctor about her son Hugo: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head"Few know the human cost of Marseille's gangs like mother Karine Brouillard - who lives at the other end of France, almost as far from the Mediterranean coast as you can get.Her son, Hugo, first ran away aged 15 - from his home in a village in the Nord department - after an argument with his family. He was picked up by police three days later, almost 1,000km (600 miles) away in Marseille, with money and cannabis on him. He was taken home.But several years later, in 2023, Hugo planned to return south, telling his parents he had secured a holiday job at a restaurant near Marseille."He gave regular updates," Karine remembers. "He called me, everything was going well."Three weeks later, a doctor called. Karine says she will never forget his words: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head."Police believe Hugo was brought for medical help from a gang-controlled area and suspect he was involved with one.That area was Quartier Nord.Image source, Lea Guedj / BBCImage caption, DZ Mafia wields power in Marseille's Quartier NordOur best way into Quartier Nord, where DZ Mafia wields power, is with the help of resident Fadella Ouidef, a 41-year-old mother-of-four who gives us a tour.Thirty-seven seconds after entering one housing estate, we find ourselves cornered.Car horns sound the moment Fadella's Peugeot passes a gang checkpoint - the teenagers manning the post immediately spot our camera. "Wait, stop filming," Fadella warns, as a grey 4x4 forces us to the side of the road."I'm making a report for my housing association," she tells the inquisitive driver. He eventually agrees to let us leave if we stop filming.It is unnerving to see a non-police vehicle move so assertively and a relief to watch it leave."Lately, the gangs have been very aggressive," explains Fadella. "What we simply try to do is make sure our young people understand what's happening is wrong."Fadella speaks to a wider fear among local families: that their children are enticed by huge sums of money to take a criminal path that robs them of their innocence.Image source, Lea Guedj / BBCImage caption, Camil, who claims to have left DZ Mafia, only agreed to speak to the BBC away from the city - on a boatMoney is what led one young man to spend his teenage years with DZ Mafia.In order for our interviewees to speak freely, or because of safety concerns, we have agreed to protect their identities.Camil tells us he worked up the gang's ranks to "running security" in one area it controls.The now 20-year-old, who claims to have left the group, is highly suspicious of our presence, but agrees to tell us how the gang recruits young members."They know how to get inside your head. Whatever you want, they give to you," he says. This can range from nice cars and spacious apartments, to drugs and prostitutes, he explains."You feel loyalty because of what they give you. You'll stay until the very end, until either death or prison."Camil also gives a sobering assessment of what happens if the gang identifies a weakness in a recruit: "They'll exploit it. You're their bitch, it's over."DZ Mafia member, Adam - not his real name - tells us he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad when we speak to him in a Snapchat video call.He is currently in prison awaiting trial, after being implicated in several murders."People noticed my determination, my cold-bloodedness and, without wanting to, I climbed up the ladder of the gang," says Adam. "It became my place, I had to roll with it."During the chat, he agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking"."Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy,  slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."Image source, Marianne Baisnee / BBCImage caption, "Thank you, see you soon" reads graffiti on a wall, alongside price lists for cocaine, hashish and marijuanaWe challenge Adam on whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality.He says he is "feeling in-part guilty" but claims to have no regrets."If I hadn't done all of this, there are other people who would have done that in my place, and so on. I am just another brick in the wall," he says.Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".At a so-called deal point in a social housing estate - sealed off and controlled by DZ Mafia - price lists for cocaine, hashish and marijuana are graffitied on a wall.The estate acts as a natural fortress for drug dealers. With one major road in and out, they can control the flow of customers and see if the police are coming.It is not uncommon for the sound of automatic gunfire to fill the night air in these areas.After months of negotiations, a deal-point manager from a rival gang agrees to meet us where he works.Image source, Lea Guedj / BBCImage caption, Gang member "Joe" says he was making €3,000 (£2,500) per month aged 13We enter the estate early in the morning, the birdsong and children walking to school providing a stark contrast to the industrial-scale criminal operation that takes place here."Joe" says he was making €3,000 (£2,500) a month when he was 13. Now he says that has risen to between €5,000 and €10,000 a month.He seems to see his life path as pre-ordained, albeit a lucrative one.We ask Joe if he thinks about the lives lost because of the violence carried out by his gang, but the 23-year-old has also long made peace with the pain and destruction drug trafficking can cause."It destroys people, but we all make our own choices," he shrugs.The work that Joe's gang and DZ Mafia are doing represents a threat to national security, says Zoulas, of the anti-drug trafficking unit.There are road accidents, as well as family violence, depressions, suicides and more than 700 overdoses each year, he says, "and it distorts the economy"."We are heading towards a potential systemic breakdown of the criminal justice system."Image source, Social mediaImage caption, DZ Mafia members filmed firing guns from a balcony in Marseille - the footage was then posted on social mediaPolice have had success in Marseille and other cities against drug gangs.Criminal operations are being frustrated, more kingpins arrested and drugs seized.Since 2024, about 1,000 individuals associated with DZ Mafia have been arrested, and 600 incarcerated, police say.But overall, it is a battle that is becoming more arduous, rather than easier.As gangs seek to widen their operations, or replace members who have been arrested or killed, social media has become a potent recruitment tool - especially since the Covid pandemic, when many street-drug sales jumped online.On social media, we found countless posts advertising jobs in Marseille for aspiring drivers, couriers and hitmen, often with glamourised AI-generated images.Nets are also being cast wider, as it becomes harder to entice young people locally because they know more about what might happen to them.The ads can reach teenagers in most corners of France - including Paris, Nantes and Lille - and serve as a powerful pull to Marseille, and the Quartier Nord, police say.Online advertising has also changed the typical profile of someone who would join a gang's ranks, say law enforcement officials.Now, it is often someone without a criminal past, but who has exploitable vulnerabilities, like having a difficult family life."These people are recruited by unscrupulous sponsors who send them into the lion's den," explains Thibaut Fontaine, the head of France's anti-organised-crime unit.Their lack of criminal experience, he says, makes them easier to arrest quickly.Karine still has no idea why her son, Hugo, was shot.Asked what she would say to gang leaders recruiting children and young men in Marseille, she says: "They destroy families. Little sisters, little brothers, grandparents. But then, I don't think those people have a heart, really."The restaurant where her son said he was going to work did exist, but staﬀ there told Karine they had never recruited anyone called Hugo. The reason for his death almost certainly lies within Marseille's Quartier Nord.Additional reporting by Marianne Baisnee, Lea Guedj and Paul Pradier

schema.headline: Inside the French drug gangs recruiting children to kill

title: Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
description: Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried
body: Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report, external. The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage."Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter."It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened the week on a positive note after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting. But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so important to the AI industry."Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993. Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him. He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision. By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.

schema.headline: Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy

title: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
description: The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the m
body: The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models."Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand. It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little. But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech."President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.It think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.We don't know when their affair began or ended, but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work. China denies that she was engaged in espionage.Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest. Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy. He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.But can he survive?At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out. Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.  He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings. And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

title: Trump questions elections integrity after previously accepting midterm results
description: US President Donald Trump has questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results in which Republicans suffered sweeping losses, days after sayi
body: US President Donald Trump has questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results in which Republicans suffered sweeping losses, days after saying he would accept the outcome."Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong?" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday. This appeared to contradict what he told the New York Times on election night that he was  "absolutely willing" to accept the results. Democrats retook both chambers of Congress in last week's elections. State and local officials across the US said voting had been mostly problem-free.Some key races, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi, have yet to be called.In the Truth Social post, Trump made vague claims about polling, voting "dumps", and "machines" without providing specific evidence of what this referred to and whether he believed there had been error or wrongdoing. The reporting of vote counts on election night proceeded as normal, according to Charles Stewart III, a political scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). "We saw across the nation the standard patterns we see in terms of when the votes are reported," he said. Stewart added that in some states, like Florida and Georgia, some initial reporting of results happens quickly because they already have the results of early and mail ballots. Trump has previously attempted to cast doubts on the integrity of elections he has lost, although he himself was not on the ballot in the midterms. "We would have won easily if I was on the ballot," Trump told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, after it was confirmed his party had lost both the Senate and the House. US midterm elections results 2026Surveys ahead of the election from several pollsters and news outlets suggested that Republicans could lose seats in both the House and Senate.As it stands, Democrats have won 54 US Senate seats and 254 US House seats in the midterms, giving them comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress even as counting continues in some races, like in Alaska and Mississippi. "State laws and practicalities are such that some states will just take longer to count," said Ruth Greenwood, director of the Election Law Clinic at Harvard Law School.  "That doesn't mean anything nefarious is occurring—we just need to trust local election officials to count every vote and tell us the results when they are done."The outcome has been clear since election night. Trump told the New York Times then: "We'll, you know, look forward to working with [Democrats]", adding: "We'll probably work something out."He has also offered his own analysis of why Republicans lost, acknowledging on Fox News that the Iran war had contributed to the defeat."People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that," he said. Vice-President JD Vance has also blamed the Iran war, which began in February and which has severely disrupted global oil and gas supplies - causing costs to soar, as the reason their party lost the election.In the run-up to the midterms, Trump made claims about widespread voting fraud, despite evidence that it is rare.He and his allies alleged for months that the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to former President Joe Biden, had been rigged against him. His lawyers and allies spent weeks attempting to litigate the results, but courts repeatedly struck them down.The justice department during his administration has made unprecedented attempts to exert more federal control over elections - a power the Constitution primarily delegates to individual states.Days before these midterms, it filed controversial lawsuits in federal courts challenging the count and certification of votes in states like California and Alaska, but judges ruled against them in nearly all instances.Election law experts, state officials, and local elections offices told the BBC they had spent months preparing for a scenario in which the White House or election sceptics questioned the votes' legitimacy.Despite the intense focus around election integrity on both sides of the debate, top state and local election officials have reported a mostly smooth process so far for the 2026 midterms.Extreme weather did force some location closures, and a handful of reported administrative or technical issues slowed the process in some local jurisdictions.

title: Republican Thomas Massie will force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth
description: A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has vi
body: A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution."By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorisation, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said.The effort will likely fail, as Republicans remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says the effort is aimed at pushing President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.Hegseth has called the impeachment effort a "sham" and defended his record."You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said in a video statement last week. "It's not going to work. We will not back down."He called Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" and said he was not concerned about the impeachment effort. In the video, Hegseth defended his leadership of the department and listed ways he has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda.Massie formally introduced his articles of impeachment in a resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon. The move starts a 48-hour clock for the chamber to take up the measure. Lawmakers could vote on the resolution directly, vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside."I'm doing this because it's the right thing to do," he told reporters after introducing the articles.Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it started nearly nine months ago. He has previously garnered headlines over demanding the Trump administration release the files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and has now brought them back in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections. He has said the effort was aimed at preventing a Democrat spectacle next year when they have control of Congress. He said he hoped to force Trump to name a replacement, who could be quickly confirmed while Republicans have power. "My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials."Democratic leadership has signalled openness to such an effort against Hegseth once they take control in January. Asked about the effort on Monday, Hegseth said, "We're not worried about that". He said he planned to hold a news conference on Tuesday to discuss the subject. Impeaching a cabinet secretary is rare. It must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office. Trump was impeached by the House twice in his first term in office but was cleared by the Senate after two trials and not removed.  As with the presidential process, the House would first hold a vote on charges against Hegseth and the Senate then would conduct a trial to decide whether to acquit or convict.The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not convict either one.While impeachment has been "an incredibly rare process", it has become far more normalised since the House impeached President Bill Clinton in 1998, said Paul Gowder, a law professor at Northwestern University in Chicago. He said it has become "much more common as the country has become more politically polarised," adding a prediction that several more of Trump's cabinet members may face impeachment over the next two years. Massie told reporters he was not sure if the measure had sufficient backing to pass. It would need a majority to pass the House and even with all Democratic support, it would still likely need some Republican support as the party holds a slim majority. Peter Loge, a professor of public affairs at George Washington University, told the BBC that he believed it was likely to pass due to those slim margins. "There are enough angry Republicans that more than enough Republicans are gonna simply not show up to vote," he said.Currently, there are 218 Republicans and 214 Democrats in the House.While the House requires a simple majority to pass articles of impeachment, the Senate mandates a two-thirds vote to convict, threshold that is difficult to meet in the current congressional term. When Democrats take over in January, they are likely to have at least 54 Senate seats - though two races do not yet have winners due to slim voting margins. A total of 60 votes will be required to convict and remove an official from office.

title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
description: Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the boss of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.The US President said he spoke with ch
body: Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the boss of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.The US President said he spoke with chief executive Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign."I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.China has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".Nvidia, who has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.But later on Monday, Trump said the FBI was now looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the probe or when it was launched. The BBC has contacted the FBI. US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia, the company at the centre at the development of AI worldwide through its microchips.The American firm run, co-founded by Huang, is also a major focus in the AI rivalry between the US and China, with officials treating the company's exports to Beijing as a matter of national security.Trump, at a Monday afternoon news conference, said he thought Huang was an "honorable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape"."I did speak to him today just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing, and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy," the president said.Trump added he was "sure" China president Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyondNvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spyWhat we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spyHuang has admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He said on Monday he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched. Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.In the letter, the chairmen of the committees said they were seeking a briefing "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".It's unclear whether Huang will appear. The BBC has contacted Nvidia and the committees.

title: Krakow shooting suspect has died in hospital, police say
description: A gunman suspected of killing six people in central Krakow, as well as his parents and sister at their home, died in hospital early on Monday, Polish
body: A gunman suspected of killing six people in central Krakow, as well as his parents and sister at their home, died in hospital early on Monday, Polish police have said.The 24-year-old, who has been named as Michal Oksinski by local media, was injured after opening fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland, on Saturday, police said.Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.Authorities initially reported that the gunman had apparently been inspired by "far-right ideologies", but have since said they are investigating any possible motivation.After the shooting, which began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's busy Main Market Square, police identified the attacker as a 24-year-old Polish man. In the hours after the shooting, a minister said that early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.However, during a press briefing on Monday morning, Przemysław Nowak, a spokesperson for Poland's National Prosecutor's Office, said investigations into his motive remain ongoing.Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed in the  attack.Four victims are Polish, while a British national and an Austrian woman were also killed.Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack.On Sunday, Polish police confirmed those three victims had been identified as the alleged gunman's 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and 21-year-old sister.Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.Four firearms were found in the gunman's car, including two AR-15 rifles and two handguns, along with several hundred rounds of ammunition, Nowak said. Authorities also seized at least four phones from his car and person, and electronic equipment from his home.Sixteen people, including five foreigners, two police officers and the attacker, were taken to hospital. The interior ministry later said they were from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia.Speaking on Sunday, one of two surgeons who treated victims on the street after the attack said his colleague "undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.The two surgeons, who were eating near the Main Market Square when the gunman opened fire, rushed to the scene to treat both the attacker and the two injured police officers. Professor Michal Pędziwiatr told the BBC: "We saw the shooting attack. And what a surgeon can do in a situation like this?... We decided to help the victims as soon as possible.""We rushed into the area where the shooting was and started our rescue, because there were no ambulances available, there were no professionals around."Pędziwiatr said his colleague, who has been named by local media as Dr Mateusz Wierdak, used his hand to stem the bleeding from the most severely injured policeman, allowing time for an ambulance to arrive.On Sunday it was reported that both injured officers had emerged from comas.Witnesses who were near the Main Market Square have described their panic and confusion as the attack unfolded. Ruby, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".She said they "just kept sprinting" until they found a hotel to shelter inside. Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover"."I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 metres away," he said.

title: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByDaniel BushWashington correspondent and Madeline HalpertRepublicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that po
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByDaniel BushWashington correspondent and Madeline HalpertRepublicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy."There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away. It's too early to tell which faction will win. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency."There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist. "But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."Image source, Getty ImagesShould Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tuesday night saw Trump's Republicans lose in states they had comfortably held for decadesDemocrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination."Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are seen as contenders for the 2028 nominationOther rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race."It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said."But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."Figure caption, 'Hopefully things get done': Americans react to historic political shiftFollow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?

title: Jensen Huang: What we know about Nvidia CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy
description: One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting
body: One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an investigation.US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.On Sunday, Huang admitted, external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company.President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is also investigating the affair. The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC.Trump said he spoke with Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign."I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters.US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported, external. Her current whereabouts are unknown.Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked.However, the BBC understands Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment.The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. She did not respond to the paper's request for comment.When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not."We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC.China has rejected the spying allegations.Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday at a regular daily press briefing: "We have already responded to this. The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China."The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf.Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy."US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman, according to the New York Times.Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race, which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers.Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China.Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech", he has a reputation as a workaholic and perfectionist with incredibly high standards for his staff.He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index."Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang.Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged."I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country".Founded by Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games. Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates. Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did, effectively building the infrastructure from scratch."Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them," Witt told the BBC.Every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure, including Amazon, Meta, Google, and Microsoft, now use Nvidia chips.Currently worth $4.5tn (£3.4tn), Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies ever.For now, the firm's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team".Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake.There is no public succession plan for the 63-year-old. He has often said he hopes to continue in the role for decades, and Bloomberg reports he has created an informal leadership structure around him unlike a traditional company's hierarchy.His children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez work at Nvidia in senior roles.Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners.They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer.In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.Witt told the BBC that Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him". "He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."Additional reporting by Tom McArthur in London, Ayeshea Perera and Tessa Wong in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney

title: Footage shows derailed carriages after fatal train crash in Egypt

body: A train collision has killed at least seven people and injured dozens in northern Egypt.Footage showed multiple overturned carriages and dozens of people surrounding them.One train was travelling from Giza to the Fayoum oasis, south west of Cairo, while the other was heading from Cairo to Aswan in the south.It is yet unclear what caused the accident but Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said an investigation was underway and would "hold accountable anyone who proves their negligence".Read more about the train collision in Egypt.
